implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent supplies the plumbing: fan out with CompletableFuture.supplyAsync on an explicit Executor, then CompletableFuture.allOf(futures).join() blocks until every partial has arrived; allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so the merged message is assembled from the individual futures' join()/get() results. For push-style arrival the aggregator object is a ConcurrentHashMap<correlationId, Partial> plus an AtomicInteger or a CompletableFuture completed by the thread that stores the last partial, and CompletableFuture.orTimeout (Java 9) or a scheduled task supplies the time-out completeness condition. The classic ExecutorCompletionService loop stays justified when results must be consumed in completion order or when a best-so-far result is published after a deadline.
pitfalls: A single failed future makes join() throw CompletionException and (without handle/exceptionally) the sibling results are never read: partial tolerance needs per-future handling.
supplyAsync without an Executor runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is sized to the CPU count - blocking asks there starve every other parallel stream in the JVM.
allOf waits for every future, including exceptionally completed ones, then itself completes exceptionally; inspect each future or handle failures before merging partial results.

variants.name: ExecutorCompletionService take/poll collector loop
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Java 5 aggregator: submit every ask to an ExecutorCompletionService and take()/poll() completed futures one by one until the completeness condition holds - all expected results or the deadline - merging as each result arrives. This is literally the Aggregator's collect-until-complete loop and is the shape to choose when partial results must be published after a time-out (best-so-far) or consumed in completion order, because allOf gives only an all-or-nothing completion and returns results in input order.
pitfalls: poll/take timeouts are per call: recompute the remaining budget against one absolute deadline, or N slow results each get the full timeout.
Results arrive in completion order, so any order-sensitive merge must re-sort by sequence number before aggregating.

A task exception surfaces at f.get(); catch it and account for it under the chosen partial-failure policy, otherwise the collector aborts before its completeness decision can handle the missing result.
